title: Violet Jessop — Miss Unsinkable, who survived Olympic, Titanic and Britannic
sources: Wikipedia: Violet Jessop (2 October 1887 – 5 May 1971), 'Miss Unsinkable' — born in Argentina to Irish parents; very ill as a child with presumed tuberculosis, doctors predicted it would be fatal; stewardess from 1908; aboard RMS Olympic on 20 September 1911 when it left Southampton and collided with the cruiser HMS Hawke — no fatalities, the ship returned to port; transferred to Titanic in April 1912, aged 24; Titanic struck an iceberg on 14 April and sank about 2 h 40 min later; she was ordered on deck to set an example for passengers who could not follow the instructions; put in lifeboat 16, Sixth Officer Moody gave her a baby to look after; rescued by Carpathia, where a woman, presumably the mother, grabbed the baby and ran off without a word; WWI Voluntary Aid Detachment nurse; aboard hospital ship Britannic on 21 November 1916 when it hit a German mine in the Aegean and sank within 55 minutes, killing 30 of 1,066; lifeboats were drawn into the propellers, she jumped out of hers and suffered a traumatic head injury; returned to work at sea in 1920 and retired in 1950; died 1971 aged 83

Wikipedia: HMHS Britannic — mine laid by U-73 near Kea; two lifeboats launched early were drawn into the still-turning propellers and destroyed, killing 30; sank at 09:07, 55 minutes after the explosion
Wikipedia: RMS Olympic — the Hawke collision tore two large holes in Olympic's hull; no one was killed
Wikipedia: Nearer, My God, to Thee — Violet Jessop said in her 1934 account that she heard the hymn being played as Titanic sank; others, such as Archibald Gracie, denied it

Photos (public domain, Wikimedia Commons / Library of Congress / US National Archives): Violet Jessop in VAD uniform; surviving Titanic stewardesses at Plymouth, 1912; RMS Olympic, 1911; Olympic and HMS Hawke after the collision; Titanic at Southampton, April 1912; a suspected iceberg photographed near the site, 1912; Willy Stöwer's painting of the sinking (1912, illustration); Titanic lifeboats on Carpathia; survivors on Carpathia; Titanic's band; HMHS Britannic, 1916
Archive film (public domain): 'Titanic Disaster — Genuine Footage (1911–1912)', Gaumont newsreels — Titanic in port, icebergs, Carpathia (watermark blurred)
Music: Nearer, My God, to Thee — United States Air Force Band, public domain

post.facebook:
She was aboard three sister ships. One crashed, one hit an iceberg, one hit a mine. She survived all three.

Violet Jessop was a stewardess on RMS Olympic, the biggest liner in the world, when it collided with the cruiser HMS Hawke in September 1911. The hull was torn open — nobody died.

Seven months later she joined Olympic's new sister: Titanic. On the night of 14 April 1912 it struck an iceberg. Violet was ordered on deck to show passengers how to stay calm, and as lifeboat 16 was lowered an officer handed her a baby. She later said she heard the band play "Nearer, My God, to Thee" — others swore they didn't. On the rescue ship Carpathia, a woman snatched the baby from her and ran off without a word.

In the First World War she became a nurse on the third sister, the hospital ship Britannic. On 21 November 1916 it hit a German mine off Greece and sank in 55 minutes. Lifeboats were sucked into the still-turning propellers; Violet jumped into the sea, hit her head badly — and survived that too.

She went back to sea for another 30 years, and died in 1971, aged 83. They called her Miss Unsinkable.

Luckiest woman alive, or cursed? 🚢

Violet Jessop, a stewardess, was on RMS Olympic when it collided with HMS Hawke in 1911, on Titanic when it sank in 1912 — handed a baby as lifeboat 16 was lowered — and, as a wartime nurse, on HMHS Britannic when it hit a mine and sank in 55 minutes in 1916. She jumped from a lifeboat being dragged toward the propellers, and survived. They called her Miss Unsinkable.
